messages.author: 55ddc415d5aca3b1
messages.subject: pcount
parts:
Hi everyone,

I'm planning to analyze replicated deer count data. Deers were counted
multiple times each year since the late 1990's in 4 populations.
Populations are closed within years, but obviously open between years.
Is there a way to run a single analysis (some kind of robust-model
pcount) possibly using dummy variables for "year" or should I run each
year separately? I couldn't really find out by looking at the
unmarkedFramePCount data structure.

Thanks for the help!

J.

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] pcount
parts:
Hi Jerome,

I think that Richard has answered a version of your question earlier. I would say that it is OK to use year as a blocking factor and estimate separate abundances for each year. What you do then is to ignore the correlation among counts at the same place in different years.

Another possibility would be to aggregate the counts within a year and use the new Dail-Madsen Open point count model, see pcountOpen().

Regards -- Marc

I've had a look at both pcountOpen() and gmultmix() and their
associated papers. I'm afraid I couldn't really decide which fits my
problem best, so maybe I'll provide some more details and soemone will
be able to help me out.
I have deer count data that have been collected along 4 transects
during 9 to 11 years. Counts were replicated each year between 3 and 7
times (many NAs). Populations are demographically closed each year but
open to recruitment and mortality between years. Availability to
detection (temporary emigration) is expected to vary each year
depending on snow level (deer populations stay hidden in the forests
when snow cover is low and move down to transect height with
increasing winter rigour). The populations under scrutiny are
therefore open to movements and demographic processes, in which case
the gmultmix() model is seemingly not appropriate if I follow
Chandler et al. (2011). Detection probability is probably influenced
by rain and fog during counts.
The Dail & Madsen pcountOpen() looks promising but I couldn't really
find out how to incorporate the primary/secondary periods in it. Has
anyone worked with a similar data structure and would be willing to
share?

Thanks for all your help!

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: [unmarked] Re: pcount
parts:
Hi Jerome,

as I understand, you can only use pcountOpen() for your pure counts (in the sense of not having any additional information about detection, such as individual detection, removal, distance).

You can fit the Dail-Madsen model to robust-design data. Look at the data-frame generating function unmarkedFramePCO() to see how to format the data and tell unmarked that you have within-year reps.

Regards -- Marc

messages.author: 527e14923215b7e4
messages.subject: Re: AW: [unmarked] Re: pcount
parts:
Hi Jerome,

Marc is right that gmultmix requires data such as removal counts or double observer counts. Eventually we might add a function to allow for simple repeated count data.

Regardless, if the population is open to demographic processes, you are better off using pcountOpen. However, if you do not have closure during the secondary periods, due to temporary emigration, then you need to be careful with how you proceed. If you assume closure, then your estimate of "p" will need to be interpreted as "the probability that an individual of the superpopulation is present and of detected" where the superpopulation refers to any deer that could possibly be detected at the survey location. Or, you could assume no closure whatsoever and estimate both within-season and among-season gain/loss parameters.  Note however that when you have no secondary periods the model is extremely sensitive to deviations from the parametric assumptions, so it's a good idea to assess model fit.

Richard

messages.author: 527e14923215b7e4
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: pcount
parts:
Hi Jerome,

This is confusing! One thing to note, primaryPeriod is optional, and you probably don't need to specify it in most cases. It is a nSite X nYear matrix indicating the primary period for a group of observation. If you have 4 sites and you surveyed them each on 3 consecutive years, then you don't need to provide this argument. The default would be:

1 2 3
1 2 3
1 2 3
1 2 3

But suppose you surveyed each site on 3 different years over a 10 year period. Then, the matrix could look something like

1 5 10 # This site was surveyed in years 1,5,10
1 2 3
4 5 6

Does that help? I'll try to improve the docs.

Richard

messages.author: 527e14923215b7e4
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: pcount
parts:
Hi Jerome,

From the help page for unmarkedFramePCO:

[y is ] An MxJT matrix of the repeated count data, where M is the number of sites, J is the maximum number of secondary sampling periods per site and T is the maximum number of primary sampling periods per site.

In your case, J=12 and T=13, so your matrix needs to have 12*13=156 columns. If your sites were only surveyed 5 times during a primary period, there will be 7 columns of missing values for that primary period. In other words, you just need to pad your current matrix with missing values. Hope this helps.

Richard
